In particular operating engine re-ignition, venting or attitude control devices results into hard ignition, erroneous forceand torque estimation and into 'ice' deposition on walls with potential damaging impact when breaking off. In order to model this complex flash-boiling process and solidification process, an integrated experimental and theoretical study shall combine synergicallydifferent disciplines and skills. An integrated comparative approach, based on detailed experiments, molecular dynamic simulations,modern molecular kinetic theory for modelling nucleation, bubble growth and evaporation processes, is a substantial leap forward with respect to the current modelling approaches that still heavily rely on empirical correlations or quasi-equilibrium assumptions. Experimentally, non-intrusive velocity and droplet size measurements in flash-boiling sprays, separation of ice particle areas from liquid droplet areas and visualization of the internal injector/orifice flow are envisaged, paired by systematic and controlled experiments on dropwise condensation/evaporation. These sets of experiments will provide then the basis for the development and validation of a comprehensive physical model, capable of describing and predicting the behaviour of cryogenic flashing jets. Theoretically, accurate models will be proposed to describe the evolution of the bubble size distributions within the nozzle flow (or liquid jets),the fragmentation process and the process of superheated dropwise evaporation. For the theoretical analysis, different approaches will be used: direct and approximated solutions of the Boltzmann equations, molecular dynamic simulations and the kinetic theory of homogeneous nucleation. The final goal is to include kinetic effects in the formulation of macroscopic models to improve the accuracyofthe predictions for large departure from equilibrium (i.e., at highly superheated conditions).
